_: The verify gate's pure rules, as DATA — one file, three runners (SPEC.md §3.1).
Why this exists: the three implementations agreed by DISCIPLINE. Each MUST in the spec had
hand-written twin tests in Rust and Scala and a hand-written script for ScalaScript, and every
fix was ported by hand — BUG-026 landed in Rust alone and needed a second and third pass, which
is how a contract kept in three places stops being one contract.
Every case carries `why`: the measurement that put it here. A case with no incident behind it is

shell_lex.why: BUG-018 (2026-08-04): asked for one string, the model merged `cargo run -- 3 4` into a single argument and failed a correct program.
The same afternoon, the other direction: one quoted argument split into five.
Single quotes group too; a task may use either.
Runs of whitespace are one separator, and the edges are not empty arguments.
An explicitly empty argument is an argument — the quotes are what say so.
Nothing lexes to nothing, not to one empty word.

A task is markdown. Measured 2026-08-13 on the matrix's own rpn prompt: the trailing backtick stuck to the last argument, the arity rule matched nothing, and the guard written for exactly this task was silently inactive.

task_states.task: write a program that prints olleh
task_states.why: The ordinary case: the task says what it must print, so the check may demand it.

task_states.task: read words.txt and print the top three words by count
task_states.why: BUG-026 (2026-08-05): three lines appearing nowhere in the task, invented by the model and then demanded by the check. No correct program can pass it — 0/4 before the guard, 3/3 after.
Whitespace-insensitive on purpose: a task writes `prints olleh` and a model answers `olleh\n`.
Case-insensitive for the same reason — the model reflows what the task wrote.
An empty expectation cannot be looked up in the task. `checkable: false` is the right answer there, and the guard must not turn emptiness into agreement.

task_argv_for.task: Verify BOTH: `cargo run -- "3 4 + 5 *"` must print 35, and `cargo run -- "5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -"` must print 14.
task_argv_for.why: The matrix's rpn task, verbatim. This is the case the arity rule exists for, and it did not fire until the backtick rule landed.

task_argv_for.task: build an rpn calculator. `cargo run -- "3 4 + 2 *"` must print 14
task_argv_for.why: The quotes in the TASK are the arity. The prose after the example never enters.

task_argv_for.task: add two numbers: cargo run -- 3 4 prints 7
task_argv_for.why: The same rule in the other direction — two words, two arguments.

task_argv_for.task: write a program that prints olleh
task_argv_for.why: No `cargo run --` example in the task, so there is no arity to take from it and the model's own list stands. Null is a real answer, not a failure.

task_argv_for.task: run it as `cargo run -- 3 4` and it prints 7
task_argv_for.why: Nothing to match: an empty value cannot select a prefix, and guessing one would invent an argument list.
